name: Jandoquile v. Revilla, Jr.
subject: Legal and Judicial Ethics
facts: Atty. Quirino P. Revilla, Jr., a notary public, notarized a complaint-affidavit signed by three people: Heneraline L. Brosas (the sister of his wife), Herizalyn Brosas Pedrosa (his wife's sister-in-law), and Elmer L. Alvarado (the live-in houseboy of the Brosas family). He did not ask any of them to show valid ID cards. Bernard N. Jandoquile filed a complaint asking the Supreme Court to disbar him. Atty. Revilla, Jr. admitted the facts. He argued that this single act is not a ground for disbarment, that he acted more as the three signers' lawyer than as a notary public, and that he did not need their IDs because he knows them personally.
issue: Should Atty. Revilla, Jr. be disbarred for (1) notarizing a complaint-affidavit signed by relatives of his wife, and (2) not asking the signers to show valid ID cards?
ruling: No disbarment, but he was penalized. (1) He violated the disqualification rule in Section 3(c), Rule IV of the 2004 Rules on Notarial Practice, because two of the signers are his relatives within the fourth civil degree of affinity (relatives through marriage). He should have refused to notarize. The Court rejected his claim that he acted as their lawyer and not as a notary public: the notarial certificate at the bottom of the document bore his signature as a notary public. (2) He was not liable for skipping the IDs. A notary public who knows the signers personally need not ask for their IDs, as shown by the definition of a jurat. But he was at fault for not stating in the jurat that he knows them personally. (3) His violation was not deceit, malpractice, gross misconduct, gross immoral conduct, or any other serious ground for disbarment under Section 27, Rule 138 of the Rules of Court. Since disbarment should not be imposed when a lighter penalty will do, he was reprimanded and disqualified from being commissioned as a notary public, or from performing any notarial act, for three months. He was also told to inform the Court by affidavit once those three months are over.
keyDoctrine: A notary public may not notarize a document if the principal (the person whose act is being notarized) is a relative by affinity or consanguinity within the fourth civil degree, even if the notary is also that person's lawyer. A notary who personally knows the signers need not ask for their IDs, but should say in the jurat that they are personally known. A single violation like this is not a ground for disbarment; a lighter penalty is enough.

name: Zulueta v. Court of Appeals
subject: Mercantile Law
facts: Cecilia Zulueta is the wife of Dr. Alfredo Martin. On March 26, 1982, she entered her husband's medical clinic and, in the presence of her mother, a driver, and his secretary, forcibly opened the drawers and cabinet there. She took 157 documents and papers: private letters between Dr. Martin and his alleged mistresses, greeting cards, cancelled checks, diaries, his passport, and photographs. She wanted to use them as evidence in the case she had filed against him for legal separation and for disqualification from practicing medicine. Dr. Martin sued to get the papers back and for damages. The trial court ruled for him, ordered her to return the papers, made her pay damages, and barred her and her lawyers from using the papers as evidence. The Court of Appeals agreed. Zulueta's only argument before the Supreme Court was that in an earlier disbarment case against her lawyer (Martin v. Felix, Jr.), the Court had already ruled these papers admissible as evidence.
issue: Are the papers that the wife took from her husband's clinic, without his knowledge and consent, admissible as evidence, on the theory that the Court already held them admissible in the earlier disbarment case against her lawyer?
ruling: No. The petition was denied. (1) The earlier case did not decide that the papers were admissible. The lawyer was cleared in that case only because, when he used the papers, the trial court's order banning their use was temporarily stopped by the Supreme Court's restraining order (TRO). Once that TRO was lifted, the ban applied again. (2) The papers are inadmissible. The Constitution says the privacy of communication and correspondence is inviolable, and this applies even when the person who violated it is the wife. The only exceptions are a lawful order of the court, or when public safety or order requires otherwise, as prescribed by law. Evidence obtained in violation of this is inadmissible for any purpose in any proceeding. (3) Marriage does not take away a person's right to privacy. The intimacies between husband and wife do not justify either one breaking into the other's drawers and cabinets to look for evidence of infidelity. The law protects free communication between spouses by making it privileged, but freedom of communication is different from forcing each spouse to share everything they know with the other. **A wife's taking of her husband's private papers violated his privacy of communication; the papers were inadmissible.**
keyDoctrine: The constitutional right to privacy of communication and correspondence (1987 Constitution, Art. III, Sec. 3) applies even between husband and wife. Evidence obtained in violation of it is inadmissible for any purpose in any proceeding. The only exceptions are a lawful order of the court, or when public safety or order requires otherwise, as prescribed by law. A person does not give up their right to privacy by getting married.

name: Spouses Hing v. Choachuy, Sr.
subject: Mercantile Law
facts: Spouses Bill and Victoria Hing own a lot in Mandaue City, Cebu. Next to it is a building of Aldo Development & Resources, Inc. (Aldo), where an auto-repair shop operates. Aldo had earlier sued the Hings, claiming their fence construction would destroy its wall, but that court denied Aldo's request for an injunction (a court order to stop an act) for lack of proof. The Hings then sued Alexander Choachuy, Sr. and Allan Choachuy. They said that, to gather evidence for Aldo's case, the Choachuys installed two video surveillance cameras on Aldo's building facing the Hings' property, and had employees take pictures of the Hings' construction without consent. The Choachuys said they did not install the cameras and were only stockholders of Aldo, not its owners. After an ocular inspection (the judge visited and viewed the site), the trial court ordered them to remove a revolving camera that viewed the Hings' lot and move it elsewhere. The Court of Appeals annulled that order. It reasoned that the Civil Code's protection of the privacy of one's residence did not apply because the property was not used as a residence, and that the Choachuys, as mere stockholders, could not have installed the cameras.
issue: (1) Did installing surveillance cameras facing the Hings' property violate their right to privacy, even though the property was not used as a residence? (2) Were the Choachuys the proper parties to be sued, even though Aldo, not they, owned the building?
ruling: The petition was granted and the trial court's injunction was reinstated. (1) Yes, there was a violation. The right to privacy is simply 'the right to be let alone.' Article 26(1) of the Civil Code forbids prying into the privacy of another's residence, but it also covers 'similar acts.' Following Tolentino, a business office is entitled to the same privacy when the public is excluded and only allowed persons may enter. So the protection covers places, locations, or even situations a person considers private, as long as society recognizes that right. Courts use the 'reasonable expectation of privacy' test, a two-part test: (a) did the person, by their conduct, show an expectation of privacy; and (b) is that expectation one society recognizes as reasonable. This is decided case by case. Surveillance cameras should not cover places where there is a reasonable expectation of privacy unless the affected person consents, and should not be used to pry into another's residence or business office, which would be no different from eavesdropping, a crime under R.A. No. 4200 (Anti-Wiretapping Law). The Hings had a reasonable expectation of privacy in their property, whether used as a business office or residence, so cameras facing it or covering a significant part of it without their consent clearly violated their privacy. (2) Yes, the Choachuys were proper parties. Not owning the building does not mean they did not cause the cameras to be installed. Aldo is a family corporation managed by the Choachuy family, there was a long-running boundary dispute between the two families, and the Choachuys let the court inspect the building and argued that Aldo would be damaged if the cameras were moved. They were using Aldo's separate corporate personality as a shield.
keyDoctrine: The right to privacy under Article 26(1) of the Civil Code is not limited to a residence. It extends to places where a person has the right to exclude the public, like a business office. Whether privacy was violated is decided by the 'reasonable expectation of privacy' test: (1) did the person, by their conduct, show an expectation of privacy, and (2) is that expectation one society recognizes as reasonable. Surveillance cameras may not cover places where there is a reasonable expectation of privacy without the affected person's consent.

name: Vivares v. St. Theresa's College
subject: Mercantile Law
facts: Julia and Julienne, both minors, were graduating high school students at St. Theresa's College (STC) in Cebu City. In January 2012, while changing into swimsuits for a beach party, they and others took pictures of themselves in their undergarments. Another student, Angela, uploaded the pictures to her Facebook profile. Escudero, an STC computer teacher, learned about the photos from her students. Using STC's computers, those students logged into their own Facebook accounts and showed her more photos of the girls, including photos of them drinking and smoking in a bar and walking the streets in clothes that showed their brassieres. The students said that at times these photos were viewable by any Facebook user. Escudero reported this to STC's discipline officer. STC found that the girls broke the Student Handbook and barred them from the graduation ceremony. Julia's mother (Vivares) and Julienne's parents (the Suzaras) then filed a petition for a writ of habeas data (a court remedy to protect a person's information privacy). They said the girls' Facebook accounts were set to 'Friends Only,' that Escudero intruded into the accounts and saved and showed the photos without consent, and that STC spread them by attaching them to its court papers in a related case. The trial court dismissed the petition.
issue: Should a writ of habeas data be issued? More specifically, was there an actual or threatened violation of the minors' right to privacy when STC viewed and used the Facebook photos?
ruling: No. The petition was denied. (1) Procedural points: The writ of habeas data is not limited to cases of extralegal killings and enforced disappearances. It is an independent remedy to enforce the right to informational privacy. Also, the person or entity sued need not be in the business of gathering data. To be 'engaged' in gathering, collecting, or storing data just means doing or taking part in it. (2) The right to informational privacy is the right of individuals to control information about themselves. Having an expectation of privacy is not incompatible with using online social networks (OSNs) like Facebook. But a user must first show the intention to keep a post private by using the OSN's privacy tools. Using these tools is how a person claims informational privacy online. (3) Here, the girls did not prove they limited who could see the photos. Their claim that only five people could see them was self-serving. They did not dispute that the girls' Facebook friends showed the photos using their own accounts, with no special means. Since Facebook's default setting is 'Public,' the photos may be presumed viewable by everyone. Even a 'Friends Only' setting does not make a post very private, because friends can share posts or tag others, which widens the audience. STC officials were mere recipients of photos voluntarily shown by people who had legitimate access to them. They used no unlawful means, and attaching the photos to court papers was not a privacy violation. The result might have been different if the photos had been set to 'Only Me' or a 'Custom' list. (4) On cyber responsibility: internet users must be careful and use privacy tools if they want to keep information private. The Court cannot protect people who did nothing to put the matter within their private zone.
keyDoctrine: The right to informational privacy is the right to control information about oneself. A social media user has a reasonable expectation of privacy only if they show the intention to keep a post private by using the platform's privacy tools to limit who can see it. A 'Public' or even 'Friends Only' post is not automatically private. A writ of habeas data needs proof, at least by substantial evidence, of an actual or threatened violation of the right to privacy in life, liberty, or security. It is not limited to extralegal killings and enforced disappearances.

name: Cadajas v. People
subject: Mercantile Law
facts: Christian Cadajas, 24, met AAA, 14, at the canteen where he worked. They chatted on Facebook Messenger and became sweethearts in April 2016. AAA's mother, BBB, learned of the relationship because AAA used BBB's phone to access her Facebook account and sometimes forgot to log out. BBB disapproved and told Cadajas to stay away because AAA was a minor. In November 2016, BBB read messages in which Cadajas coaxed AAA into sending him photos of her breasts and vagina, which AAA did. AAA rushed to a computer shop to delete the messages, but BBB forced her to open Cadajas's Facebook Messenger account (AAA had his password) to get a copy of the conversation. Cadajas was charged with child pornography under Section 4(c)(2) of R.A. No. 10175 (Cybercrime Prevention Act), in relation to R.A. No. 9775 (Anti-Child Pornography Act). The trial court convicted him, and the Court of Appeals affirmed. Before the Supreme Court, he argued that the photos and messages were inadmissible because they were taken from his Facebook Messenger account in violation of his right to privacy.
issue: (1) Were the photos and messages taken from Cadajas's Facebook Messenger account inadmissible because they were obtained in violation of his right to privacy? (2) Was he guilty of child pornography committed through a computer system?
ruling: The petition was denied, and the penalty was increased to reclusion perpetua. (1) The evidence was admissible. The constitutional rule that evidence obtained in violation of the privacy of communication is inadmissible (Art. III, Sec. 3) protects people against the government, not against other private individuals. Here the evidence was obtained by a private person, not by the police or any agent of the State. The Court said its statement in Zulueta v. Court of Appeals about inadmissibility between spouses was a mere obiter dictum (a side remark that is not a binding precedent). Privacy violations between private individuals are governed by the Civil Code, the Data Privacy Act, and other laws, and admissibility is governed by the Rules on Evidence. The evidence was properly authenticated when AAA identified it in court. The Data Privacy Act also allows processing of sensitive personal information when it relates to determining criminal liability, or when necessary to protect lawful rights in court proceedings. Applying the 'reasonable expectation of privacy' test from Spouses Hing v. Choachuy, Sr., there was no privacy violation: Cadajas voluntarily gave AAA his password, which limited his expectation of privacy as to her. It does not matter that her mother forced her to open it. In any case, he did not object to the photos at trial when they were formally offered, so his objection was waived. (2) He was guilty. The elements were proven: AAA was a child; he induced her to produce child pornography; and it was done through electronic means. The sweetheart defense does not apply to child pornography. The crime is mala in se (wrong in itself), so criminal intent must be proven, and his intent was shown. Since it was committed through a computer system, the penalty is one degree higher than under R.A. No. 9775.
keyDoctrine: The Bill of Rights' exclusionary rule on privacy of communication (Art. III, Sec. 3(2) of the Constitution) applies only to evidence obtained by the State or its agents, not by private individuals. Privacy violations between private persons are governed by the Civil Code, the Data Privacy Act, and other laws, while admissibility is governed by the Rules on Evidence. A person who voluntarily gives someone else their account password limits their reasonable expectation of privacy as to that person. The Data Privacy Act allows processing of sensitive personal information when it relates to determining criminal liability or is needed to protect lawful rights in court proceedings.

name: Regala v. Sandiganbayan
subject: Mercantile Law
facts: In 1987 the Republic, through the Presidential Commission on Good Government (PCGG), sued Eduardo Cojuangco, Jr. and others before the Sandiganbayan to recover alleged ill-gotten wealth, including shares in several corporations. Also sued were lawyers who were partners of the ACCRA Law Firm, including Teodoro Regala, Edgardo Angara, and Raul Roco, plus Paraja Hayudini, who had left the firm. As part of their legal services, ACCRA lawyers helped clients organize and acquire companies and, following office practice, acted as nominee-stockholders (holding shares in their own names for clients). They gave clients the stock certificates endorsed in blank and blank deeds of trust or assignment. The PCGG dropped Roco from the case because he supposedly promised to reveal the identity of the client for whom he acted as nominee. The other ACCRA lawyers asked for the same treatment. The PCGG said it would drop them only if they (a) disclosed the identity of their clients, (b) submitted documents showing the lawyer-client relationship, and (c) submitted the deeds of assignment they executed in favor of their clients. The lawyers refused, invoking the attorney-client privilege, and the Sandiganbayan denied their request to be excluded. (The petition of Hayudini, G.R. No. 108113, was decided together with this one.)
issue: (1) Can the ACCRA lawyers refuse to reveal the identity of their clients on the ground of attorney-client privilege? (2) Did dropping Roco but not the other lawyers violate the equal protection clause?
ruling: The Sandiganbayan resolutions were annulled, and it was ordered to exclude the petitioning lawyers from the case. (1) Yes, the lawyers may refuse. The lawyers were sued only to pressure them into naming their clients, so the PCGG could go after the 'bigger fish.' Their inclusion was based only on services they performed as lawyers, so the PCGG had no valid cause of action against them. The general rule is that a lawyer may not refuse to reveal a client's identity. The reasons: the court has a right to know the client is real, the privilege exists only once there is a client, the privilege covers the subject matter of the relationship, and an opposing party is entitled to know who their opponent is. But there are exceptions. Client identity is privileged: (a) where there is a strong probability that revealing the client's name would implicate the client in the very activity for which they sought the lawyer's advice; (b) where disclosure would open the client to civil liability; and (c) where the client's name would furnish the only link that would form the chain of testimony needed to convict the client of a crime. In short, a client's identity is privileged when the name itself has an independent significance, such that disclosing it would reveal client confidences. This case falls under at least two exceptions. The PCGG's conditions showed that the clients consulted the lawyers about the corporate set-up in question, so naming them would implicate them in the very activity for which they sought advice and would supply the missing link for the case against them. The Court distinguished between a client who hires a lawyer to plan an illegal act (not privileged) and a client who thinks they may have already done something illegal and asks a lawyer about it (privileged). The privilege also continues even after the lawyer-client relationship ends. (2) Yes, equal protection was violated. There was no proof that Roco actually revealed his client's identity, and he and the others were similarly situated. The PCGG's demand also violated the lawyers' right against self-incrimination and was a 'fishing expedition.'
keyDoctrine: As a general rule, a lawyer may not refuse to reveal a client's identity. But the identity is privileged when the client's name has an independent significance, such that disclosing it would reveal client confidences. Examples: (1) a strong probability that revealing the name would implicate the client in the very activity for which legal advice was sought; (2) disclosure would open the client to civil liability; or (3) the name is the only link needed to form the chain of testimony to convict the client. The privilege does not protect a client who seeks advice in order to commit a future illegal act.

name: Integrated Bar of the Philippines v. Purisima
subject: Mercantile Law
facts: In 2014, Finance Secretary Cesar Purisima, on the recommendation of BIR Commissioner Kim Jacinto-Henares, issued Revenue Regulations No. 4-2014 to monitor the service fees of self-employed professionals. It required them to: (a) submit an affidavit stating their rates, manner of billing, and the factors they consider in setting fees; (b) register their books of account and their official appointment books, which would contain only the clients' names and the date and time of each meeting; and (c) issue a BIR-registered receipt showing a 100% discount for pro bono (free) services. The Integrated Bar of the Philippines (IBP) and the Association of Small Accounting Practitioners in the Philippines challenged the regulation before the Supreme Court. The Philippine College of Physicians, Philippine Medical Association, and Philippine Dental Association joined. They argued that it violated their clients' and patients' right to privacy and their professions' rules on confidentiality, and that it went beyond what the Tax Code allows. The Office of the Solicitor General later sided with the petitioners on some points. The government argued that only names and appointment dates would be disclosed, which are not privileged.
issue: Do the requirements of Revenue Regulations No. 4-2014, especially the mandatory registration of appointment books, violate the right to privacy of professionals and their clients and patients, and the confidentiality rules of their professions?
ruling: The petitions were partly granted. (1) Registering books of account and issuing receipts for pro bono services are valid. (2) The affidavit of rates, billing, and fee factors is void because it goes beyond the Tax Code. It serves no legitimate purpose, although it does not encroach on the Court's rule-making power or violate ethical norms. (3) The mandatory registration of appointment books is void because it is an unconstitutional intrusion into the right to privacy. The Court explained that privacy covers 'zones of privacy' and three strands: locational, informational, and decisional privacy. Informational privacy is the right to control the processing (acquisition, disclosure, and use) of personal information. To decide whether a government intrusion is impermissible, the court asks whether the person showed a reasonable expectation of privacy and, if so, whether it was violated by unreasonable government intrusion. Clients and patients reasonably expect privacy when they set appointments with professionals. Examples: a battered wife who does not want it known she is seeing a lawyer, or a patient seeing a specialist. Names and dates alone 'paint no picture,' but as Disini v. Secretary of Justice teaches, gathered together they can reveal a pattern of behavior, and that pattern is protected. The mere chance that the State may look into this information is already an unreasonable intrusion. (4) The requirement also violates professional confidentiality. Citing Regala v. Sandiganbayan, a client's identity may be privileged in proper cases, so the government was wrong to say names are never privileged. The Data Privacy Act generally prohibits processing sensitive personal information and privileged information, which includes privileged communications under the Rules of Court, except in the cases listed in Section 13. Physician-patient communications are also privileged, and accountants' working papers are confidential under the Philippine Accountancy Act. The DOF and BIR were permanently stopped from implementing the void parts.
keyDoctrine: Requiring self-employed professionals to register appointment books containing their clients' or patients' names and meeting times is an unconstitutional intrusion into the right to privacy. Clients and patients have a reasonable expectation of privacy in their consultations. Even if names and dates alone reveal little, put together they can show a protected pattern of behavior, and the mere chance that the State may look at them is an unreasonable intrusion. Under the Data Privacy Act, processing privileged information, including privileged communications under the Rules of Court, is generally prohibited except in the cases listed in Section 13.
